entry.title: Why Batch Norm struggles inside transformers!

link.title: Why Batch Norm struggles inside transformers!

entry.content:
Open a ResNet and there’s a BatchNorm2d after nearly every convolution. Open a GPT-style model and you get LayerNorm (or its cousin RMSNorm) in front of every attention and MLP block. On paper the two do the same job: subtract a mean, divide by a standard deviation, apply a learned scale and shift. So why did the two families of models end up with different ones?

In an earlier #BehindTheBasics post I gave the short answer: it comes down to which axis you compute the statistics over. Batch Norm compares a feature with the same feature in the other samples of the batch. Layer Norm looks at one sample and nothing else. My analogy was grading. Batch Norm grades on a curve, so your mark depends on who else sat the exam; Layer Norm marks each paper on its own.

The axis part I’d still defend. Everything around it was too quick, and two of that post’s claims don’t hold up: Batch Norm in an LLM does not “divide by zero” at batch size 1, and Layer Norm in a CNN does not automatically wreck accuracy. The tidy rule “images get Batch Norm, text gets Layer Norm” has been broken from both ends, too. ViT and ConvNeXt run Layer Norm on images, and most open LLMs since LLaMA use RMSNorm instead of Layer Norm.

This is the long version. I’ll go through the claims one at a time and look at each from four sides: where the norm sends a vector, what it makes the model blind to, the derivation, and a code cell you can run (every number quoted in the text is one those cells printed). The thread through all of it is that the five layers are one formula applied over different axes of the same tensor. Once you can see the geometry of those axes, the rule of thumb falls out, and so do its exceptions.

Here’s the grading analogy stretched to cover four of the five norms:

One formula, five choices of axes

Everything starts from two tensor shapes. After a convolution, a CNN’s activations have shape \((N, C, H, W)\): \(N\) images, \(C\) channels, and an \(H \times W\) grid of positions. A transformer’s have shape \((B, T, D)\): \(B\) sequences, \(T\) token positions, and a \(D\)-dimensional vector per token. A normalization layer picks some set \(S\) of these axes, takes the mean and variance over them, and uses those two numbers to standardize every entry that shares them.

To write that down, let \(x\) be one entry and \(S(x)\) the group of entries it shares statistics with, meaning everything that matches \(x\) on the axes not in \(S\). Then

\[\begin{gathered} \mu_S = \frac{1}{|S(x)|} \sum_{x' \in S(x)} x', \\ \sigma_S^2 = \frac{1}{|S(x)|} \sum_{x' \in S(x)} (x' - \mu_S)^2, \\ y = \gamma \, \frac{x - \mu_S}{\sqrt{\sigma_S^2 + \epsilon}} + \beta . \end{gathered}\]

\(\epsilon\) is a small constant (PyTorch’s default is \(10^{-5}\)) that keeps the division finite. \(\gamma, \beta\) are a learned scale and shift, one per channel or feature, which let the network undo the normalization if it wants to. One detail matters if you ever check your own code against PyTorch: the variance is the biased one, divided by \(\lvert S(x)\rvert\) and not \(\lvert S(x)\rvert - 1\). Every library norm layer does it this way.

With the formula fixed, the five layers differ only in \(S\):

Layer Tensor \(S\) (axes averaged over) One mean and variance per
Batch Norm \((N, C, H, W)\) \(N, H, W\) channel
Layer Norm (CNN form) \((N, C, H, W)\) \(C, H, W\) image
Layer Norm (transformer) \((B, T, D)\) \(D\) token
Instance Norm \((N, C, H, W)\) \(H, W\) image and channel
Group Norm \((N, C, H, W)\) \(C/G, H, W\) (one group of channels) image and group
RMSNorm \((B, T, D)\) \(D\), and no mean subtraction token

Only Batch Norm puts the batch axis in its \(S\). The other four compute their statistics inside a single sample, and most of this post comes back to that one difference.

Here is the same formula with its parts labelled. Only the statistics change from layer to layer; the small constant and the learned scale and shift play the same role in all five.

And the animated version, if you’d like to watch the shaded set move around while the formula stays put:

Time for code. Cell 1 pins the versions I tested with, seeds every random generator and keeps everything on the CPU, so your printed numbers should match mine.

%pip install -q "torch==2.13.0" "numpy==2.3.3" "matplotlib==3.10.8" "scikit-learn==1.6.1"
import math
import random
import statistics

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F
from sklearn.datasets import load_digits

SEED = 0
random.seed(SEED); np.random.seed(SEED); torch.manual_seed(SEED)
torch.set_num_threads(1)  # every model here is tiny; one thread is faster and keeps numbers reproducible
torch.set_printoptions(precision=4, sci_mode=False)
device = "cpu"            # CPU on purpose: the printed numbers match for every reader
print(f"torch {torch.__version__} | numpy {np.__version__} | device={device}")

torch 2.13.0+cpu | numpy 2.3.3 | device=cpu

Cell 2 turns that table into code. normalize(x, axes) is the formula with \(\gamma = 1, \beta = 0\), and its argument axes is \(S\). Group Norm needs one reshape first: split the \(C\) channels into \(G\) groups so that “one group of channels” becomes an axis you can average over. RMSNorm is the same call with center=False. Each line is checked against the matching PyTorch layer, and the cell prints the worst disagreement.

def normalize(x: torch.Tensor, axes: tuple[int, ...], eps: float = 1e-5, center: bool = True) -> torch.Tensor:
    """(x - mean_S) / sqrt(var_S + eps), where S = `axes`. center=False gives RMSNorm."""
    mu = x.mean(dim=axes, keepdim=True) if center else 0.0
    var = ((x - mu) ** 2).mean(dim=axes, keepdim=True)  # biased variance, as every norm layer uses
    return (x - mu) / torch.sqrt(var + eps)

N, C, H, W, G = 8, 6, 5, 5, 3
x = torch.randn(N, C, H, W) * 3 + 1
ours = {
    "BatchNorm":    (normalize(x, (0, 2, 3)), "N, H, W"),
    "LayerNorm":    (normalize(x, (1, 2, 3)), "C, H, W"),
    "InstanceNorm": (normalize(x, (2, 3)), "H, W"),
    "GroupNorm":    (normalize(x.view(N, G, C // G, H, W), (2, 3, 4)).view_as(x), "C/G, H, W"),
    "RMSNorm":      (normalize(x, (1, 2, 3), center=False), "C, H, W (no centering)"),
}
reference = {
    "BatchNorm":    nn.BatchNorm2d(C, affine=False).train()(x),
    "LayerNorm":    nn.LayerNorm((C, H, W), elementwise_affine=False)(x),
    "InstanceNorm": nn.InstanceNorm2d(C)(x),
    "GroupNorm":    nn.GroupNorm(G, C, affine=False)(x),
    "RMSNorm":      nn.RMSNorm((C, H, W), eps=1e-5, elementwise_affine=False)(x),
}
print(f"{'norm':<14}{'averages over':<25}{'max |ours - torch|':>18}")
for name, (y, axes_text) in ours.items():
    print(f"{name:<14}{axes_text:<25}{(y - reference[name]).abs().max().item():>18.1e}")

tokens = torch.randn(4, 7, 16)  # (B, T, D): a transformer's activations
print("transformer LayerNorm == normalize over D only:",
      torch.allclose(normalize(tokens, (2,)), F.layer_norm(tokens, (16,)), atol=1e-6))

norm          averages over            max |ours - torch|
BatchNorm     N, H, W                             4.8e-07
LayerNorm     C, H, W                             3.6e-07
InstanceNorm  H, W                                3.6e-07
GroupNorm     C/G, H, W                           4.8e-07
RMSNorm       C, H, W (no centering)              2.4e-07
transformer LayerNorm == normalize over D only: True

All five match PyTorch to within \(5 \times 10^{-7}\) (the worst gap, 4.8e-07, is for Batch Norm and Group Norm), which is just float32 rounding. I find this the most satisfying output in the post. Five library classes, each with its own constructor arguments, reduce to a four-line function with a single knob, axes. The last line covers the transformer case: F.layer_norm on a \((B, T, D)\) tensor is normalize over the last axis alone, and the check prints True. Every later cell reuses this function, so whenever two norms behave differently below, the axes tuple is the only thing that changed.

Layer Norm is a projection onto a sphere

Take a single token’s vector \(x \in \mathbb{R}^d\) and run Layer Norm on it with \(\gamma = 1, \beta = 0\) and, for now, \(\epsilon = 0\). Two things happen, and both have a clean picture.

First, centering. It turns out to be a projection. Let \(\mathbf{1} = (1, 1, \dots, 1)\) be the all-ones vector in \(\mathbb{R}^d\), and note that the mean of \(x\)’s entries is \(\mu = \frac{1}{d}\mathbf{1}^\top x\), so

\[x - \mu \mathbf{1} = \Big(I - \tfrac{1}{d}\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^\top\Big)\, x = P x .\]

Look at the matrix \(P = I - \frac{1}{d}\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^\top\). It’s symmetric, it satisfies \(P^2 = P\), and it sends \(\mathbf{1}\) to zero (\(P\mathbf{1} = \mathbf{1} - \mathbf{1} = 0\)). That makes it an orthogonal projection onto the hyperplane \(\mathbf{1}^\perp = \{z : z_1 + \dots + z_d = 0\}\). In words: centering slides \(x\) along \(\mathbf{1}\) until its coordinates add up to zero, then forgets how far it slid.

The second step, dividing by the standard deviation, lands the vector on a sphere. The variance is the mean squared entry of the centered vector, \(\sigma^2 = \frac{1}{d}\lVert P x \rVert^2\), so \(\sigma = \lVert Px \rVert / \sqrt{d}\) and

\[\begin{gathered} \mathrm{LN}(x) = \frac{P x}{\sigma} = \sqrt{d}\, \frac{P x}{\lVert P x \rVert}, \\ \lVert \mathrm{LN}(x) \rVert = \sqrt{d} . \end{gathered}\]

Every output has length \(\sqrt{d}\), however long the input was. Put the two steps together and Layer Norm drops \(x\) onto the hyperplane \(\mathbf{1}^\perp\), then pushes it out to the sphere of radius \(\sqrt{d}\) inside that hyperplane, which is a \((d-2)\)-dimensional sphere. Each token loses exactly two numbers, its mean and its scale, and keeps its direction within \(\mathbf{1}^\perp\). The learned \(\gamma\) and \(\beta\) then stretch the sphere into an ellipsoid and move it, so the next layer always receives a fixed, learned shape instead of activations of whatever size happened to come in.

RMSNorm skips the first step. Zhang & Sennrich (2019) argued that re-centering contributes little to Layer Norm, so they dropped it and divided by the root mean square in place of the standard deviation:

\[\begin{gathered} \mathrm{RMS}(x) = \sqrt{\tfrac{1}{d}\textstyle\sum_i x_i^2} = \frac{\lVert x \rVert}{\sqrt{d}}, \\ \mathrm{RMSNorm}(x) = \frac{x}{\mathrm{RMS}(x)} = \sqrt{d}\,\frac{x}{\lVert x \rVert} . \end{gathered}\]

The length is still \(\sqrt{d}\), but the output can now sit anywhere on the full \((d-1)\)-dimensional sphere; Layer Norm’s outputs were confined to the slice of it that lies in \(\mathbf{1}^\perp\). RMSNorm throws away the scale and keeps the mean. It’s cheaper too: one reduction (the sum of squares) against Layer Norm’s two (the mean, then the variance).

Cell 3 tests both claims on 300 points in \(d = 3\). In three dimensions the “sphere inside the plane” is a circle of radius \(\sqrt{3} \approx 1.7321\) in the plane \(x + y + z = 0\), which is small enough to actually plot. I set eps=0.0 because the epsilon is the only thing that would nudge the lengths away from \(\sqrt{3}\).

points = torch.randn(300, 3) * torch.tensor([2.0, 0.7, 1.2]) + torch.tensor([1.5, -1.0, 0.5])
ln_points = normalize(points, (1,), eps=0.0)                 # each point (row) on its own
rms_points = normalize(points, (1,), eps=0.0, center=False)  # RMSNorm: rescale only
for name, p in [("LayerNorm", ln_points), ("RMSNorm", rms_points)]:
    norms = p.norm(dim=1)
    print(f"{name:<10} max |x+y+z| = {p.sum(1).abs().max():.2e} | ||y|| in [{norms.min():.4f}, {norms.max():.4f}]")
print(f"sqrt(d) = sqrt(3) = {math.sqrt(3):.4f}")

u = torch.tensor([1.0, -1.0, 0.0]) / math.sqrt(2)  # orthonormal basis of the plane x+y+z=0
v = torch.tensor([1.0, 1.0, -2.0]) / math.sqrt(6)
t = torch.linspace(0, 2 * math.pi, 200)
circle = math.sqrt(3) * (torch.outer(t.cos(), u) + torch.outer(t.sin(), v))
fig = plt.figure(figsize=(14, 4.6))
panels = [("raw points", points), ("LayerNorm: plane x+y+z=0, radius sqrt(3)", ln_points),
          ("RMSNorm: radius sqrt(3), off the plane", rms_points)]
for k, (title, p) in enumerate(panels, 1):
    ax = fig.add_subplot(1, 3, k, projection="3d")
    ax.scatter(*p.T, s=6, alpha=0.6)
    if k > 1:
        ax.plot(*circle.T, color="crimson", lw=2)
    lim = 4.5 if k == 1 else 2.0
    ax.set(xlim=(-lim, lim), ylim=(-lim, lim), zlim=(-lim, lim), xlabel="x", ylabel="y", zlabel="z", title=title)
    ax.set_box_aspect((1, 1, 1))
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

LayerNorm  max |x+y+z| = 1.61e-06 | ||y|| in [1.7321, 1.7321]
RMSNorm    max |x+y+z| = 2.99e+00 | ||y|| in [1.7321, 1.7321]
sqrt(d) = sqrt(3) = 1.7321

Both predictions hold to float precision. After Layer Norm, no point’s coordinates sum to more than 1.61e-06 in absolute value, so all 300 points are in the plane, and every length falls in [1.7321, 1.7321]. In the middle panel, the stretched, off-center cloud from the left has collapsed onto the red circle. RMSNorm also gives every point length 1.7321, but its coordinate sums go as high as 2.99, and in the right panel the points are spread over the sphere instead of sitting on the circle. Layer Norm took two numbers from each point (mean and scale); RMSNorm took one.

The sphere shows up in the backward pass as well. Since \(\mathrm{LN}(c\,x) = \mathrm{LN}(x)\) for any \(c > 0\), and \(\mathrm{LN}(x + b\mathbf{1}) = \mathrm{LN}(x)\) for any \(b\), nudging the input along \(x\) or along \(\mathbf{1}\) doesn’t move the output. Differentiate those two identities and you find that the gradient of the loss with respect to \(x\) is orthogonal to both \(x\) and \(\mathbf{1}\), so it lies in the tangent plane of the output sphere. Its size goes as \(1/\lVert Px \rVert\), which means inputs with large activations get proportionally smaller gradients. Xu et al. (2019) found that these backward-pass effects (the gradients flowing through \(\mu\) and \(\sigma\)) matter more for training than the forward normalization itself. I’m skipping the derivation for this one and just showing the result:

Batch Norm reshapes the cloud

Now take a whole batch: \(B\) samples with \(d\) features each, stacked into a matrix \(X \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times d}\) with one sample per row and one feature per column. Layer Norm works row by row, applying the projection-and-sphere map to each sample on its own. Batch Norm works column by column. For feature \(j\) it computes

\[\begin{gathered} \mu_j = \frac{1}{B}\sum_{i=1}^{B} X_{ij}, \\ \sigma_j^2 = \frac{1}{B}\sum_{i=1}^{B} (X_{ij} - \mu_j)^2, \\ \hat X_{ij} = \frac{X_{ij} - \mu_j}{\sqrt{\sigma_j^2 + \epsilon}} . \end{gathered}\]

The picture I find most useful is a cloud of \(B\) points in \(\mathbb{R}^d\). Batch Norm slides the whole cloud so its centroid is at the origin, then stretches or squeezes it along each coordinate axis until the spread along every axis is 1. That’s a single affine map, \(x \mapsto D^{-1}(x - \mu)\) with \(D = \mathrm{diag}(\sigma_1, \dots, \sigma_d)\), applied to every sample alike.

Because everyone gets the same map, two things survive it. Relative positions survive: a sample far out to the right of the cloud is still far out to the right afterwards, so Batch Norm erases nothing about an individual sample and only re-expresses each feature as “standard deviations from the batch average”. Correlations survive too, because Batch Norm scales the axes and never rotates them. Removing correlations would take the full inverse square root of the covariance matrix, \(\Sigma^{-1/2}\) (whitening), and Batch Norm only has the diagonal \(D^{-1}\). A tilted, stretched cloud comes out still tilted.

Training and evaluation are different stories. During training, \(\mu_j\) and \(\sigma_j\) come from the current batch, so a sample’s output depends on which other samples it happened to share a batch with. Batch Norm also keeps running averages, updated after each training batch as \(\hat\mu_j \leftarrow (1 - m)\,\hat\mu_j + m\,\mu_j\) with momentum \(m = 0.1\) in PyTorch (and the same for the variance). In evaluation mode (model.eval()) it switches to those running statistics and becomes a fixed per-feature affine map, \(y_j = \gamma_j (x_j - \hat\mu_j)/\sqrt{\hat\sigma_j^2 + \epsilon} + \beta_j\), which doesn’t look at the batch at all. Hold on to this one, because it comes back later: a trained Batch Norm model can run inference on one sample at a time without any trouble.

Cell 4 runs both norms on the same 200-sample, 2-feature batch. Two dimensions is a deliberately extreme case for Layer Norm. With \(d = 2\) the hyperplane \(\mathbf{1}^\perp\) is the line \(x_1 + x_2 = 0\), and the “sphere of radius \(\sqrt{2}\)” inside a line is just two points, \((1, -1)\) and \((-1, 1)\). Keep an eye on the three colored samples.

gen = torch.Generator().manual_seed(0)
mixing = torch.tensor([[2.0, 0.0], [1.2, 0.6]])  # correlated features with very different scales
cloud = torch.randn(200, 2, generator=gen) @ mixing.T + torch.tensor([2.0, 1.0])
bn_cloud = normalize(cloud, (0,), eps=0.0)  # columns: one feature across the batch
ln_cloud = normalize(cloud, (1,), eps=0.0)  # rows: one sample on its own

def corr(z: torch.Tensor) -> float:
    return torch.corrcoef(z.T)[0, 1].item()

print(f"correlation: raw {corr(cloud):.3f} | after BN {corr(bn_cloud):.3f}")
print(f"after BN: column means {bn_cloud.mean(0).abs().max():.1e}, column stds {bn_cloud.std(0, unbiased=False).tolist()}")
print("after LN: distinct outputs", sorted({tuple(round(v, 4) + 0.0 for v in row) for row in ln_cloud.tolist()}))

marked = [0, 1, 2]  # follow three samples through both norms
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(14, 4.4))
for ax, (title, z) in zip(axes, [("raw batch (rows = samples)", cloud), ("BatchNorm: per column", bn_cloud),
                                 ("LayerNorm: per row (d = 2)", ln_cloud)]):
    ax.scatter(z[:, 0], z[:, 1], s=10, alpha=0.4, color="gray")
    for i, c in zip(marked, ["crimson", "royalblue", "darkorange"]):
        ax.scatter(z[i, 0], z[i, 1], s=70, color=c, edgecolor="black", zorder=3)
    ax.axhline(0, color="black", lw=0.5); ax.axvline(0, color="black", lw=0.5)
    ax.set(title=title, xlabel="feature 1", ylabel="feature 2", aspect="equal")
axes[2].plot([-1.5, 1.5], [1.5, -1.5], "--", color="crimson", label="x1 + x2 = 0 (where LN outputs live)")
axes[2].set(xlim=(-1.6, 1.6), ylim=(-1.6, 1.6)); axes[2].legend(loc="upper right", fontsize=8)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

correlation: raw 0.874 | after BN 0.874
after BN: column means 7.6e-08, column stds [1.0, 1.0]
after LN: distinct outputs [(-1.0, 1.0), (1.0, -1.0)]

Batch Norm behaves the way the column picture says it should. Each column ends up with mean 7.6e-08 and standard deviation 1.0, and the correlation between the two features is 0.874 before and 0.874 after. In the middle panel the cloud has moved to the origin and changed units, but its shape hasn’t changed, and the red, blue and orange points sit in the same order as on the left.

Layer Norm maps all 200 samples to just two outputs: (-1.0, 1.0) and (1.0, -1.0). In two dimensions a sample keeps one bit, whether its first feature is bigger than its second, and all three colored samples land on the same point. That looks brutal, but it’s what happens in every dimension, only easier to see here: Layer Norm strips each sample’s own offset and scale. In \(d = 768\) you still keep 766 degrees of freedom, which is plenty. The two you lose are gone for good, though, and whether that matters is the next question.

What each norm makes your model blind to

I think the clearest way to tell these layers apart is by what they ignore, and one identity covers every case. Take the entries that share statistics, \(S(x)\), and replace each one with \(a x' + b\), using the same \(a > 0\) and \(b\) for the whole group. Then \(\mu_S \to a\mu_S + b\) and \(\sigma_S \to a\sigma_S\), so

\[\frac{(a x + b) - (a\mu_S + b)}{a\,\sigma_S} = \frac{x - \mu_S}{\sigma_S} .\]

With \(\epsilon = 0\) the output doesn’t move at all. So a norm layer is blind to any positive scale and any shift that’s constant across its group \(S(x)\). RMSNorm doesn’t subtract a mean, which makes it blind to the scale \(a\) but not to the shift \(b\). With \(\epsilon > 0\) the blindness is only approximate: once \(a\sigma_S\) becomes comparable to \(\sqrt{\epsilon}\), the output starts to change.

Read the groups off the first table and you get a concrete list:

Layer Blind to (in training) Image example Token example
Batch Norm one scale and shift per channel, shared by the whole batch the same exposure change applied to every image in the batch none in practice
Layer Norm \((C, H, W)\) one scale and shift per image that image’s overall brightness and contrast n/a
Instance Norm one scale and shift per image and channel that image’s color cast and per-channel contrast (its “style”) n/a
Group Norm one scale and shift per image and group of channels between Layer Norm and Instance Norm n/a
Layer Norm \((D)\) / per pixel one scale and shift per token or pixel vector each pixel’s channel vector length and offset the token vector’s length and mean
RMSNorm one scale per token n/a the token vector’s length

Batch Norm is the odd one out, twice. In training it’s blind only to changes that hit the whole batch identically, which almost never happens to a single input. In evaluation mode it’s a fixed affine map and isn’t blind to anything. Every other layer ignores some change to a single sample.

This also pins down what the original post meant when it said Layer Norm “suppresses intensity information” in a CNN. Layer Norm over \((C, H, W)\) sends a bright image and the same image at 30% brightness to identical activations, so the claim is true. What doesn’t follow is that accuracy has to drop. That depends on whether the task needs absolute intensity, and a digit classifier doesn’t; for it, this blindness works as robustness, which cell 7 measures. Instance Norm’s blindness to per-image style is why Ulyanov et al. (2016) used it for fast style transfer, where throwing that information away is the whole point.

Why should any of this help training? Ioffe & Szegedy (2015) pitched Batch Norm as a fix for internal covariate shift, the drift in each layer’s input distribution as the layers before it train. Santurkar et al. (2018) put that story to a direct test. They injected random, time-varying noise after every Batch Norm layer, creating covariate shift on purpose, and the networks still trained about as well. Their measurements point somewhere else: Batch Norm makes the loss and its gradients change more smoothly, which tolerates larger learning rates. The invariances fit that account. A layer whose output ignores the scale of its input can’t let activations blow up just by growing, and, as we saw with the sphere, the gradients shrink as the activations grow.

Why CNNs took Batch Norm

Back to grading. A curve is fair when the class is big, everyone sits the same exam, and a score on one question means the same thing for every student. A CNN trained on ImageNet-style data ticks all three boxes, and Batch Norm brings two practical perks on top.

The scores are comparable because of weight sharing. A convolution applies the same filter at every position of every image, so channel \(c\) means “how much of pattern \(c\) is here” on every image in the dataset. Pooling its statistics across images and positions pools measurements of one well-defined quantity. That’s why Batch Norm’s \(S\) for images contains \(H\) and \(W\) along with \(N\).

The class is big because each statistic is built from a lot of numbers. With \(S = \{N, H, W\}\), a channel’s mean averages \(N \cdot H \cdot W\) values, and a batch of 32 images at a \(56 \times 56\) feature map gives \(32 \times 56 \times 56 \approx 100{,}000\) values per statistic. Estimates from that many numbers are stable even at modest batch sizes and barely move from batch to batch, so the running averages used at test time match what the network saw during training.

Everyone sits the same exam because images get resized or cropped to one shape. Every entry in the batch is real data, and there’s no padding to contaminate the statistics.

Now the perks. The first is that Batch Norm costs nothing at deployment. In evaluation mode it’s a per-channel affine map, the convolution before it is linear, and the two fold into a single convolution with adjusted weights and bias, so a deployed ResNet pays nothing for its Batch Norm layers. The second is regularization. During training each image is normalized with statistics that depend on its batch-mates, which adds a small random wobble to every activation, and Ioffe & Szegedy (2015) reported that Batch Norm networks needed less Dropout.

History helped as well. Batch Norm arrived first, in 2015. Layer Norm came a year later, aimed at recurrent networks where Batch Norm was awkward to apply, and by then the standard CNN recipes were built around Batch Norm.

The weak spot is batch size. Detection and segmentation models often fit only one or two high-resolution images per GPU, and with batches that small the statistics get noisy and training and test stop matching. Wu & He (2018) introduced Group Norm for exactly this case: at batch size 2 on ImageNet, their ResNet-50 with Group Norm had 10.6% lower error than the Batch Norm version.

Why transformers took Layer Norm

Run the same checklist on text and it fails on every line.

First you have to decide what Batch Norm even means for a \((B, T, D)\) tensor. The natural choice, and the one Shen et al. (2020) used, averages over the batch and time axes together, \(S = \{B, T\}\): one mean and variance per feature, pooled over every position of every sequence. That choice runs into four separate problems.

The obvious one is padding. Sentences have different lengths, so to stack sentences of length 6, 4, 5 and 3 into one tensor you pad them all to a shared length \(T\), usually with zeros (or a padding embedding), and a naive Batch Norm counts those positions as data. Say the batch has \(n = B \cdot T\) positions, \(p\) of them padding zeros, and call \(f = p/n\) the padding fraction. Zeros add nothing to a sum, so for a feature whose real tokens have mean \(\mu_r\) and mean square \(m_r = \mathbb{E}_r[x^2]\),

\[\begin{gathered} \mu_{\text{batch}} = (1 - f)\,\mu_r, \\ \sigma^2_{\text{batch}} = (1 - f)\,m_r - (1 - f)^2 \mu_r^2 . \end{gathered}\]

Both statistics depend on \(f\), and \(f\) depends on how long the other sentences in the batch are. So the same token gets a different value in a different batch. You can mask the padding out, but that only moves the problem: each feature’s statistics then depend on how many real tokens the batch happens to contain.

Causality is the second problem. In a causal language model, position \(t\) must never see tokens after \(t\). With \(S = \{B, T\}\), the mean and variance used at position \(t\) include every later token in the batch, so training leaks information about the future back into the past through the statistics. At generation time the future tokens don’t exist yet, and that information simply isn’t there.

Then there’s the data itself. Shen et al. (2020) measured the batch statistics of transformers trained on text and found they swing far more from batch to batch than in image models, with large outliers. Running averages built from statistics like that don’t match any individual batch well, and the authors tied those swings to Batch Norm’s poor results on translation.

The last problem is serving. A deployed language model batches requests from unrelated users and generates one token at a time with a key-value cache, and one user’s output must not depend on who else is in the batch. Layer Norm guarantees that by construction: its \(S\) is \(\{D\}\), so each token is normalized using only its own vector.

Layer Norm sidesteps all four, because its statistics never cross a token boundary. Padding, sequence length, batch composition and causality can’t reach it. To me that’s the real reason transformers took Layer Norm. The layer has to ignore everything outside one token, and the per-token norms (Layer Norm and RMSNorm) are the only members of the family whose group \(S(x)\) stays inside one token.

Cell 5 checks the padding formula numerically. Four sequences of lengths 6, 4, 5 and 3 (18 real tokens, every feature averaging about 2) get zero-padded to longer and longer lengths \(T\), the way a tokenizer does with padding="max_length". The cell follows one fixed token (position 0 of sequence 0, feature 0) and prints three things for it: its Batch Norm output with statistics over \(B\) and \(T\), what the formula predicts, and its Layer Norm output with statistics over \(D\).

Now for the batch-size-1 claim. The original post said Batch Norm in an LLM fine-tuned at batch size 1 computes a variance of zero, divides by zero, and crashes. The zero variance happens only in one special case, and the division by zero never happens. There are really four situations, and cell 6 checks each of them.

With a single sample and no other axis in \(S\), every feature’s variance really is zero, and PyTorch refuses to continue in training mode; it raises an error. If you compute it by hand anyway, \(x - \mu = 0\) exactly, and \(\epsilon\) holds the denominator at \(\sqrt{\epsilon} > 0\), so the result is \(\gamma \cdot 0 / \sqrt{\epsilon} + \beta = \beta\) for every input. Nothing divides by zero and nothing explodes. The output just stops carrying any information about the input.

In a transformer, though, \(S = \{B, T\}\), so a single sequence of 12 tokens still gives 12 values per feature and a variance that isn’t zero. And at inference Batch Norm uses its running statistics, so batch size 1 is fine there too, unless those statistics were computed on padded batches.

To test that last case, the cell trains only the running statistics of a Batch Norm layer on 200 padded batches (8 sequences of random length 4 to 32, padded to 32, padding counted), then evaluates it on real tokens.

D = 8

    nn.BatchNorm1d(D).train()(torch.randn(1, D))      # one token, no other axis to average over
except ValueError as err:
    print("nn.BatchNorm1d on a batch of 1 ->", err)

gamma, beta = torch.full((D,), 2.0), torch.full((D,), 0.5)
one = torch.randn(1, D) * 3 + 1
manual = gamma * normalize(one, (0,)) + beta          # var = 0 and x - mu = 0: eps avoids 0/0, output is beta
print("manual BN at batch 1: every output equals beta ->", torch.allclose(manual, beta.expand_as(manual)))

for _ in range(200):                                  # training: padded batches, padding counted as tokens

All four situations show up in the output. PyTorch’s nn.BatchNorm1d raises Expected more than 1 value per channel when training, an explicit error and not a numerical crash, and the hand-computed version returns \(\beta\) for every feature (True). A single 12-token sequence has a smallest per-feature variance of 0.370, comfortably above zero.

The last two lines are the failure that actually matters. The real tokens have mean 2.00, but the running mean learned from padded batches is 1.12. On average 56% of each training batch was real data, and \(0.56 \times 2 \approx 1.12\), just as the padding formula says. Batch Norm promised outputs with mean 0 and standard deviation 1; on real tokens at inference it delivers mean 0.71 and standard deviation 0.81. Every activation leaving this layer at test time is off by about 0.7 standard deviations from what the next layer saw in training. So Batch Norm in a language model doesn’t crash. It computes the wrong statistics, and different wrong statistics in training and in inference.

The swaps, and where the rule of thumb breaks

The original post made two predictions about swapping the layers: Layer Norm in a CNN loses accuracy, and Batch Norm in a transformer breaks. The last two cells try both swaps on problems small enough to train on a laptop CPU in under a minute. These are toys, and I want to be upfront about it. They can tell us whether a mechanism exists and which way it pushes, not how big the effect is on ImageNet or a real LLM.

The CNN swap

For the CNN I used scikit-learn’s digits dataset: 1,797 grayscale handwritten digits at \(8 \times 8\) pixels. It ships with the library, so there’s nothing to download. 1,400 images go to training and 397 to testing. The model is two \(3 \times 3\) convolutions, each followed by a norm layer and a ReLU, then a linear classifier. The convolutions have no bias, which is standard when a norm layer comes next and also makes the first convolution exactly linear in the image (that will matter in a minute). I compared four norms:

  • BN: nn.BatchNorm2d, \(S = \{N, H, W\}\).
  • LN (C,H,W): Layer Norm over the whole feature map. nn.GroupNorm(1, C) computes exactly this, because one group holding all channels means \(S = \{C, H, W\}\).
  • GN (4 groups): Group Norm, \(S = \{C/4, H, W\}\).
  • LN per pixel: the variant ConvNeXt (Liu et al., 2022) uses. It normalizes each pixel’s \(C\)-channel vector on its own, the image version of a transformer’s per-token Layer Norm.

Each norm trains twice, once at batch size 64 (150 steps) and once at batch size 1 (1,000 steps). The batch-64 models are then tested a second time on the test images dimmed to 30% brightness, which puts the “intensity” claim to a direct test.

digits = load_digits()                                # 1,797 8x8 images bundled with scikit-learn
images = torch.tensor(digits.images, dtype=torch.float32).unsqueeze(1) / 16.0
labels = torch.tensor(digits.target)
order = torch.randperm(len(images), generator=torch.Generator().manual_seed(0))
train_idx, test_idx = order[:1400], order[1400:]

class PixelLayerNorm(nn.Module):
    """ConvNeXt-style LN: each pixel's C channels are normalized on their own."""
    def __init__(self, channels: int) -> None:
        super().__init__()
        self.ln = nn.LayerNorm(channels)

    def forward(self, x: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
        return self.ln(x.permute(0, 2, 3, 1)).permute(0, 3, 1, 2)

NORMS = {"BN": nn.BatchNorm2d, "LN (C,H,W)": lambda c: nn.GroupNorm(1, c),  # one group = LN over (C,H,W)
         "GN (4 groups)": lambda c: nn.GroupNorm(4, c), "LN per pixel": PixelLayerNorm}

def train_cnn(norm, batch_size: int, steps: int, lr: float) -> nn.Module:
    torch.manual_seed(0)
    model = nn.Sequential(nn.Conv2d(1, 16, 3, padding=1, bias=False), norm(16), nn.ReLU(),
                          nn.Conv2d(16, 32, 3, stride=2, padding=1, bias=False), norm(32), nn.ReLU(),
                          nn.Flatten(), nn.Linear(32 * 4 * 4, 10))
    opt, g = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr), torch.Generator().manual_seed(1)
    for _ in range(steps):
        idx = train_idx[torch.randint(len(train_idx), (batch_size,), generator=g)]
        loss = F.cross_entropy(model(images[idx]), labels[idx])
        opt.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); opt.step()
    return model.eval()

@torch.no_grad()
def accuracy(model: nn.Module, brightness: float = 1.0) -> float:
    return (model(brightness * images[test_idx]).argmax(1) == labels[test_idx]).float().mean().item()

results = {}
print(f"{'norm':<15}{'batch 64':>9}{'batch 1':>9}{'batch 64, images at 30% brightness':>36}")

    results[name] = (accuracy(big), accuracy(single), accuracy(big, brightness=0.3))
    print(f"{name:<15}" + "".join(f"{a:>9.3f}" for a in results[name][:2]) + f"{results[name][2]:>36.3f}")

At batch size 64 none of the norms wrecks the CNN. Batch Norm scores 0.975, Layer Norm over \((C, H, W)\) 0.972, Group Norm 0.975, and per-pixel Layer Norm 0.982. Swapping Batch Norm for Layer Norm costs one image. A tiny model on an easy dataset can’t prove that Layer Norm matches Batch Norm on ImageNet, but that’s roughly what ConvNeXt reported at scale, and ViT has used Layer Norm on images from the start.

At batch size 1, Batch Norm is fine. All four land between 0.924 and 0.932. The original post would predict a Batch Norm failure here, and there isn’t one, for the reason cell 6 gave. With \(S = \{N, H, W\}\) and \(N = 1\), each statistic still averages over \(8 \times 8 = 64\) spatial positions. In training mode Batch Norm at batch size 1 behaves like Instance Norm, and its running averages turned out good enough for evaluation. Its small-batch problems are real, as the Group Norm result above shows, but they come from noisy statistics and train/test mismatch. A variance of zero has nothing to do with it.

The dimmed images turn the “intensity” argument around. At 30% brightness the Batch Norm model falls from 0.975 to 0.826. Layer Norm holds at 0.972, Group Norm at 0.975, and per-pixel Layer Norm moves from 0.982 to 0.980, a single image. That’s what the invariance section predicted. With no bias in the first convolution, dimming the image just scales its output by 0.3, and every per-sample norm cancels that factor before the rest of the network sees it. Batch Norm in evaluation mode is a fixed affine map calibrated on full-brightness images, so it passes the dimming straight through and every activation shifts relative to \(\beta\). Per-pixel Layer Norm drops one image, most likely because a digit’s background pixels have almost no activation in any channel, so after dimming their variance is close to \(\epsilon\) and the invariance stops being exact. So yes, Layer Norm is blind to intensity, just as the original post said. On a task that doesn’t need intensity, that blindness lets the Layer Norm models read faint digits as well as normal ones.

The transformer swap

The transformer task is synthetic, but it keeps the property that matters here: variable-length, padded batches. Each sequence has 2 to 32 tokens drawn from \(\{1, 2, 3\}\), with one token twice as likely as the other two, and the label is whichever token appears most often. Batches of 32 sequences are zero-padded to their longest member. The model is a one-block pre-norm transformer: embedding plus learned positions, two-head self-attention, an MLP, a final norm, and a mean over the real tokens. Attention ignores padding through key_padding_mask, which leaves the norm layers as the only place padding can get in. The three versions differ only in the norm class:

  • BN: TokenBatchNorm, a naive Batch Norm over \(S = \{B, T\}\) that counts padding.
  • LN: nn.LayerNorm, \(S = \{D\}\).
  • RMSNorm: nn.RMSNorm, \(S = \{D\}\) without centering.

Each trains for 400 steps with Adam. The cell prints the mean and spread of the training loss over the last 50 steps, plus the accuracy on 500 fresh test sequences in evaluation mode.

DIM, PAD = 32, 0                                       # tokens 1..3; label = the most frequent token

def make_batch(size: int, g: torch.Generator) -> tuple[torch.Tensor, torch.Tensor, torch.Tensor]:
    lens = torch.randint(2, 33, (size,), generator=g)  # lengths 2..32, padded to the longest
    toks, y = torch.full((size, int(lens.max())), PAD), torch.zeros(size, dtype=torch.long)
    for i, L in enumerate(lens.tolist()):
        probs = torch.full((3,), 0.25); probs[torch.randint(3, (1,), generator=g)] = 0.5
        toks[i, :L] = torch.multinomial(probs, L, replacement=True, generator=g) + 1
        y[i] = torch.bincount(toks[i, :L], minlength=4)[1:].argmax()
    return toks, y, toks != PAD

class TokenBatchNorm(nn.Module):
    """Naive BN for (B, T, D): statistics over every position, padding included."""
    def __init__(self, dim: int) -> None:
        super().__init__()
        self.bn = nn.BatchNorm1d(dim)

    def forward(self, x: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
        return self.bn(x.reshape(-1, x.shape[-1])).reshape(x.shape)

class TinyTransformer(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, norm) -> None:
        super().__init__()
        self.emb, self.pos = nn.Embedding(4, DIM), nn.Embedding(64, DIM)
        self.norm1, self.norm2, self.norm_out = norm(DIM), norm(DIM), norm(DIM)
        self.attn = nn.MultiheadAttention(DIM, 2, batch_first=True)
        self.mlp = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(DIM, 4 * DIM), nn.GELU(), nn.Linear(4 * DIM, DIM))
        self.head = nn.Linear(DIM, 3)

    def forward(self, toks: torch.Tensor, mask: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
        x = self.emb(toks) + self.pos(torch.arange(toks.shape[1]))
        h = self.norm1(x)
        x = x + self.attn(h, h, h, key_padding_mask=~mask, need_weights=False)[0]
        x = self.norm_out(x + self.mlp(self.norm2(x)))
        m = mask.unsqueeze(-1).float()
        return self.head((x * m).sum(1) / m.sum(1))   # mean over real tokens only

curves = {}
for name, norm in {"BN": TokenBatchNorm, "LN": nn.LayerNorm, "RMSNorm": nn.RMSNorm}.items():
    torch.manual_seed(0); g = torch.Generator().manual_seed(1)
    model = TinyTransformer(norm); opt = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), 3e-3)
    curves[name] = []
    for step in range(400):
        toks, y, mask = make_batch(32, g)
        loss = F.cross_entropy(model(toks, mask), y)
        opt.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); opt.step(); curves[name].append(loss.item())
    model.eval()
    with torch.no_grad():
        toks, y, mask = make_batch(500, torch.Generator().manual_seed(99))
        acc = (model(toks, mask).argmax(1) == y).float().mean().item()
    tail = curves[name][-50:]
    print(f"{name:<8} loss over last 50 steps: mean {statistics.mean(tail):.3f}, std {statistics.pstdev(tail):.3f} | test acc {acc:.3f}")

plt.figure(figsize=(8, 4))
for name, c in curves.items():
    plt.plot(np.convolve(c, np.ones(20) / 20, mode="valid"), label=name)  # 20-step moving average
plt.yscale("log"); plt.xlabel("training step"); plt.ylabel("loss (20-step moving average)")
plt.title("Tiny transformer, variable-length padded batches"); plt.legend()
plt.show()

LN       loss over last 50 steps: mean 0.055, std 0.054 | test acc 0.984
RMSNorm  loss over last 50 steps: mean 0.059, std 0.062 | test acc 0.986

Batch Norm doesn’t break the transformer, but it does hold it back. Over the last 50 steps its loss averages 0.119, about twice Layer Norm’s 0.055 and RMSNorm’s 0.059, and it’s the noisiest of the three (standard deviation 0.091 against 0.054 and 0.062). In the plot all three fall together for the first 20 or so steps. After that the Batch Norm curve flattens out around 0.12 to 0.15 while the other two keep going down. Test accuracy is 0.976 for Batch Norm against 0.984 and 0.986, a gap of four to five sequences out of 500. The task is easy enough that all three solve it, which is why the difference shows up in the training curve. It’s the same direction Shen et al. found on real translation tasks, where Batch Norm in a transformer worked, just worse.

Layer Norm and RMSNorm are hard to tell apart. Their curves almost overlap for all 400 steps, and their losses (0.055 and 0.059) and accuracies (0.984 and 0.986) are within noise of each other. Dropping the projection onto \(\mathbf{1}^\perp\) cost nothing I could measure. That’s Zhang & Sennrich’s argument in miniature, and the same argument moved most LLMs to the cheaper layer.

So “images get Batch Norm, text gets Layer Norm” is a proxy for something else. What it really says is: use Batch Norm when statistics shared across the batch are reliable, which takes large, fixed-shape batches of comparable samples, and use a per-sample norm when they aren’t. Images usually meet that bar and text usually doesn’t. When images don’t (tiny batches, detection, a ViT that treats an image as a sequence of patch tokens), the per-sample norms take over on images too. Here’s the whole decision on one page:

Where the field is now

Language models have mostly moved to RMSNorm. LLaMA (Touvron et al., 2023) normalizes the input of every transformer sub-layer with RMSNorm, and most open-weight LLMs released since have copied that design. So the original post’s “LLMs use Layer Norm” was true of GPT-2-era models and is now true only in spirit: still per token, just without the centering.

Image models use whatever their batch allows. Classic CNN recipes still use Batch Norm, for the reasons in the CNN section. ViT uses Layer Norm on each patch token, ConvNeXt swapped Batch Norm for per-pixel Layer Norm in a modernized ResNet, and Group Norm is the usual pick when a detection or segmentation model fits only a few images per device.

Some recent work pushes the sphere picture much further. nGPT (Loshchilov et al., 2024) keeps every hidden vector, and every embedding and weight vector, on the unit hypersphere throughout the network, and reports reaching the same accuracy in 4 to 20 times fewer training steps. Layer Norm uses that geometry inside one layer; nGPT makes it the design principle of the whole model.

Other work gets rid of the statistics altogether. Transformers without Normalization (Zhu et al., 2025) replaces every norm layer with Dynamic Tanh, \(\mathrm{DyT}(x) = \gamma \tanh(\alpha x) + \beta\), an elementwise squashing function with a learned \(\alpha\) and no mean or variance anywhere, and reports matching normalized transformers across several tasks. Stronger Normalization-Free Transformers (Chen et al., 2025) searches over functions like that and reports that \(\mathrm{erf}(\alpha x + s)\) does better than Layer Norm, RMSNorm and DyT. On the CNN side, NFNets (Brock et al., 2021) reached strong ImageNet results without normalization by clipping gradients adaptively. If these results hold up at scale, the question this post started with stops being “which axis?” and becomes “do we need statistics at all?”. I don’t think that’s settled yet.

Batch Norm’s weak spots have their own fixes. Batch Renormalization (Ioffe, 2017) corrects batch statistics toward the running averages when batches are small or non-i.i.d., and PowerNorm (Shen et al., 2020) relaxes Batch Norm’s zero-mean constraint and uses running statistics in the forward pass so that it works in transformers.

I’ve left out one related question: where the norm sits, as opposed to which axes it averages over. Xiong et al. (2020) show that putting Layer Norm before each sub-layer (Pre-LN) instead of after the residual addition (Post-LN, the original Transformer) lets transformers train without a learning-rate warm-up.

Here’s the one-line version. All five layers compute the same formula, and picking a norm means picking \(S\). Put the batch axis in \(S\) only when the batch is a trustworthy sample of the data; otherwise keep \(S\) inside one sample. The geometry tells you what that costs: two numbers per vector with Layer Norm, one with RMSNorm.

Further reading

  • Ioffe & Szegedy (2015), “Batch Normalization: Accelerating Deep Network Training by Reducing Internal Covariate Shift”: the original Batch Norm paper, including the running statistics and the inference-time formula.
  • Ba, Kiros & Hinton (2016), “Layer Normalization”: introduces per-sample normalization and its invariances, written with recurrent networks in mind.
  • Zhang & Sennrich (2019), “Root Mean Square Layer Normalization”: the case for dropping re-centering, which is the “skip the projection” step in this post.
  • Wu & He (2018), “Group Normalization”: the clearest treatment of the BN / LN / IN / GN family as choices of axes, with the small-batch experiments.
  • Shen et al. (2020), “PowerNorm: Rethinking Batch Normalization in Transformers”: measurements of why batch statistics misbehave on text.
  • Santurkar et al. (2018), “How Does Batch Normalization Help Optimization?”: the experiment that separated Batch Norm’s benefit from internal covariate shift.
  • Zhu et al. (2025), “Transformers without Normalization”: the most direct current challenge to the idea that transformers need a norm layer at all.

entry.title: If Weight Quantization Degrades Reasoning, Why Is It the Industry Standard for LLM Scaling?

link.title: If Weight Quantization Degrades Reasoning, Why Is It the Industry Standard for LLM Scaling?

entry.content:
If you’ve ever pulled an open large language model (LLM) onto your laptop, you’ve probably seen a name like gemma3:4b-it-q4_K_M and hit enter without a second thought. The “4b” means 4 billion parameters, “it” means instruction-tuned, and q4_K_M is llama.cpp’s medium 4-bit format. Ollama lists the same Gemma 3 4B model at 8.6 GB in 16-bit and 3.4 GB as q4_K_M: about 60% smaller, and it fits on machines the full version won’t.

So what was in those missing 5 GB? Most of the weights went from 16-bit numbers to roughly 4-bit ones, with far fewer values to choose from. That has to cost something. In a quick chat you may never notice, but research on quantized reasoning models finds that below 4 bits, the hardest problems are where accuracy goes first.

Yet quantized weights are everywhere in production, from 8-bit formats in datacenters to 4-bit on laptops and phones. Part of the reason is hardware. A 70B model needs 140 GB for its 16-bit weights, and NVIDIA’s H100, the datacenter GPU much of the industry runs on, has 80 GB. You can’t even load that model on one card without shrinking it first.

So lower precision costs reasoning, and the industry runs on it anyway. Why? Below, we’ll see what quantization does to a weight, how that damage reaches reasoning, and why the industry takes the deal regardless, from post-training quantization (PTQ) to quantization-aware training (QAT), plus FP8 (8-bit floating point) serving, KV-cache quantization and on-device models.

You only need a rough idea of what a transformer layer is and how training works. There’s runnable code along the way, and the notes for running it in Google Colab come right before the first snippet.

The paradox and the bet

Whatever lets a model keep an argument straight lives in the fine differences between its weights, and a 4-bit weight can take one of only 16 values. But generating text is limited by how fast you can read weights out of memory, so the useful question is: what’s the best model I can fit in the memory I’ve got? Asked that way, a big model at 4 bits usually beats a smaller one at 16 bits (Dettmers & Zettlemoyer, 2022). Quantization is a bet on scale. Most models make it with PTQ; labs that can’t afford to lose reasoning make it with QAT, more and more often in mixed precision.

What weight quantization actually is

Models are usually trained in BF16 (bfloat16, short for “brain floating point”) or FP16 (standard 16-bit floating point). BF16 spends 1 bit on the sign, 8 on the exponent and 7 on the mantissa, and that exponent lets it represent tiny and huge values with roughly the same relative precision. Integer formats don’t have one, so INT8 and INT4 (8-bit and 4-bit integers) are evenly spaced grids of 256 and 16 values. FP8 sits in between; its E4M3 variant uses 4 exponent bits and 3 mantissa bits.

Quantizing a tensor means picking a grid and snapping every weight to its nearest point. Symmetric absmax (absolute-maximum) quantization, the simplest scheme, sets the step size \(\Delta\) from the largest weight on the grid:

\[\Delta = \frac{\max_i |w_i|}{2^{b-1}-1}, \qquad q_i = \operatorname{clip}\!\left(\operatorname{round}\!\left(\frac{w_i}{\Delta}\right),\, -(2^{b-1}-1),\, 2^{b-1}-1\right), \qquad \hat w_i = \Delta\, q_i\]

Here \(b\) is the bit width, \(w_i\) the original weight, \(q_i\) the stored integer code (−7 to 7 for INT4), and \(\hat w_i\) the value the model computes with. Asymmetric schemes add a zero-point \(z\), \(\hat w_i = \Delta(q_i - z)\), and nothing below changes. Grid points sit \(\Delta\) apart, so no weight moves more than half a step:

\[|w_i - \hat w_i| \le \frac{\Delta}{2}\]

Hold on to that inequality, because it’s the whole cost model. Precision lost scales with \(\Delta\), \(\Delta\) is set by the largest value on the grid, and going from 8 to 4 bits makes \(\Delta\) about 18 times bigger.

One more choice: how many weights share a \(\Delta\). Per-tensor uses one scale for the whole matrix and per-channel one per output row. Group-wise, the default for 4-bit LLM weights, gives each block of \(g\) weights its own scale (usually \(g = 128\)) for 0.125 extra bits per weight. Dettmers & Zettlemoyer found small block sizes were one of only two changes that reliably improved the bits-versus-accuracy trade-off.

Running the code in Google Colab

Every snippet in this post is ready to paste into a free Google Colab notebook. Here’s all the setup you need:

  • Open a new notebook at colab.research.google.com and sign in with any Google account. The free tier is enough.
  • Keep the default CPU (central processing unit) runtime. The code is plain NumPy, so the free tier’s T4 GPU wouldn’t speed anything up; under Runtime → Change runtime type, CPU is the right choice. If a GPU runtime is already selected, the code still runs, just on the CPU.
  • There’s nothing else to configure: no files to upload, no downloads and no API (application programming interface) keys. The only libraries are NumPy and matplotlib, which Colab preinstalls, and cell 1 installs them anyway if they’re missing, so the snippets also work in any fresh Python 3.10+ notebook.
  • Paste each snippet into its own cell and run them in order, because later cells reuse functions and variables from earlier ones. If the runtime disconnects, start again from cell 1.
  • The whole run takes about a minute and peaks at roughly 300 MB of memory, a small fraction of what the free tier gives you.

Cell 1 sets up that environment.

# Tested with numpy 2.0.2 to 2.4.6 and matplotlib 3.8.4 to 3.11.2: identical results.
# Google Colab already ships both, so this line normally installs nothing and needs no runtime restart.
%pip install -q "numpy>=2.0" "matplotlib>=3.8"
import matplotlib
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

SEED = 0
np.random.seed(SEED)
rng = np.random.default_rng(SEED)
np.set_printoptions(precision=4, suppress=True)
plt.rcParams.update({"figure.figsize": (8, 3.6), "figure.dpi": 120,
                     "axes.spines.top": False, "axes.spines.right": False})
print(f"numpy {np.__version__} | matplotlib {matplotlib.__version__} | seed={SEED}")

numpy 2.3.3 | matplotlib 3.10.8 | seed=0

The %pip line only installs NumPy and matplotlib if they’re missing or older than the minimum versions, so on Colab it’s normally a no-op and never asks you to restart. After that come the imports, a fixed random seed (0) so every run produces the same numbers, rng, the random generator the later cells draw from, and a few print and plot settings.

Running it prints a single line with your library versions and the seed. Don’t worry if your versions differ from mine: I ran the whole post on NumPy 2.0.2 through 2.4.6 and matplotlib 3.8.4 through 3.11.2, including a fresh environment where cell 1 had to install both, and every cell printed exactly the same numbers.

Cell 2 turns the equations into code and tests the \(\Delta/2\) bound.

def quantize(w: np.ndarray, bits: int, group_size: int | None = None) -> tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray]:
    """Symmetric absmax quantization. Returns integer codes and one scale (Δ) per group."""
    qmax = 2 ** (bits - 1) - 1                      # INT8 -> 127, INT4 -> 7
    flat = w.reshape(-1, group_size) if group_size else w.reshape(1, -1)
    scale = np.abs(flat).max(axis=1, keepdims=True) / qmax   # Δ: the grid's step size
    codes = np.clip(np.round(flat / scale), -qmax, qmax)
    return codes, scale

def fake_quant(w: np.ndarray, bits: int, group_size: int | None = None) -> np.ndarray:
    """Quantize then dequantize: the float weights a low-bit model effectively uses."""
    codes, scale = quantize(w, bits, group_size)
    return (codes * scale).reshape(w.shape)

W = rng.normal(0.0, 0.02, size=(512, 2048))         # a typical-looking LLM weight matrix
for bits in (8, 4):
    codes, delta = quantize(W, bits)
    err = np.abs(W - fake_quant(W, bits))
    print(f"INT{bits}: levels={len(np.unique(codes)):3d}  Δ={delta.item():.5f}  "
          f"max|err|={err.max():.5f} <= Δ/2={delta.item() / 2:.5f}: {err.max() <= delta.item() / 2 + 1e-12}  "
          f"MSE={np.mean(err ** 2):.2e}")

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.hist(W.ravel(), bins=200, density=True, alpha=0.5, label="original (BF16-like)")
vals, counts = np.unique(fake_quant(W, 4), return_counts=True)
ax.vlines(vals, 0, counts / counts.max() * ax.get_ylim()[1], colors="crimson", label="INT4 grid (bar height = count)")
ax.set(xlabel="weight value", ylabel="density", title="16-bit weights collapse onto 15 INT4 levels")
ax.legend(); plt.show()

INT8: levels=235  Δ=0.00079  max|err|=0.00039 <= Δ/2=0.00039: True  MSE=5.16e-08
INT4: levels= 15  Δ=0.01428  max|err|=0.00714 <= Δ/2=0.00714: True  MSE=1.70e-05

Two small functions do the work. quantize sets each group’s step \(\Delta\) (scale in the code) to the group’s largest absolute value divided by the largest code (127 for INT8, 7 for INT4), then rounds every weight to an integer code \(q\). fake_quant multiplies the codes back by the step to get \(\hat w\). The rest of the cell quantizes a 512 × 2048 matrix drawn from \(\mathcal N(0, 0.02^2)\), a typical scale for LLM weights, to INT8 and INT4, prints the levels used, step size, largest error and MSE (mean squared error) for each, and plots the original weights against the INT4 values.

Both printed lines end in True. The worst error really is exactly \(\Delta/2\). INT4’s step (0.01428) is 18 times INT8’s (0.00079), and since squared error grows with \(\Delta^2\), INT4’s MSE (1.70e-05) is about 330 times INT8’s (5.16e-08). In the plot, a smooth blue bell curve collapses onto a handful of red spikes.

Why quantization degrades reasoning

Why should an error that small matter? A dot product sums thousands of those \(\Delta/2\) errors, and the sum acts like noise on every layer’s output. At INT8 it’s negligible. At INT4 it isn’t, and it reaches reasoning in three ways.

Outliers stretch the grid

Real LLM numbers aren’t well-behaved Gaussians. Dettmers et al. (2022) found that by roughly 6.7B parameters, a handful of hidden dimensions carry “emergent outlier features” in every layer: values far larger than the rest that dominate attention and the model’s predictions. Since \(\Delta\) is set by the largest value on the grid, an outlier \(k\) times bigger than its neighbours makes \(\Delta\) roughly \(k\) times bigger, and once \(\Delta/2\) exceeds a typical weight, nearly everything rounds to zero. Strictly, those features live in the activations. W4A16 (4-bit weights, 16-bit activations) lets them pass straight through, while W8A8 (8-bit weights and activations) has to quantize them. Weights have milder outliers of their own, and the arithmetic is identical.

Cell 3 plants an artificial outlier and measures the damage.

W_out = W.copy()
W_out[:, 7] *= 20                                    # one input channel 20x larger, like an LLM outlier feature
normal = np.ones_like(W, dtype=bool); normal[:, 7] = False

def report(name: str, w_hat: np.ndarray, delta: float) -> tuple[float, float]:
    mse = np.mean((W_out[normal] - w_hat[normal]) ** 2)        # error on the *ordinary* weights
    zeroed = np.mean(w_hat[normal] == 0) * 100
    print(f"{name:<32} Δ={delta:.4f}  ordinary weights -> 0: {zeroed:5.1f}%  MSE={mse:.2e}")
    return mse, zeroed

_, d_clean = quantize(W, 4)
_, d_out = quantize(W_out, 4)
print(f"outlier stretched per-tensor Δ by {d_out.item() / d_clean.item():.1f}x\n")
cases = {
    "clean, per-tensor INT4": (fake_quant(W, 4), d_clean.item()),
    "outlier, per-tensor INT4": (fake_quant(W_out, 4), d_out.item()),
    "outlier, group-wise INT4 (g=128)": (fake_quant(W_out, 4, 128), np.median(quantize(W_out, 4, 128)[1])),
}
results = {k: report(k, w_hat, d) for k, (w_hat, d) in cases.items()}   # g=128 row shows the median Δ

fig, (a1, a2) = plt.subplots(1, 2)
labels, colors = ["clean\nper-tensor", "outlier\nper-tensor", "outlier\ngroup-wise g=128"], ["grey", "crimson", "seagreen"]
a1.bar(labels, [m for m, _ in results.values()], color=colors)
a1.set(yscale="log", ylabel="MSE on ordinary weights (log)")
a2.bar(labels, [z for _, z in results.values()], color=colors)
a2.set(ylabel="% ordinary weights rounded to 0")
for a in (a1, a2): a.tick_params(axis="x", labelsize=8)
fig.suptitle("One outlier channel vs. INT4 scaling granularity"); fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()

outlier stretched per-tensor Δ by 15.0x

clean, per-tensor INT4           Δ=0.0143  ordinary weights -> 0:  27.9%  MSE=1.70e-05
outlier, per-tensor INT4         Δ=0.2148  ordinary weights -> 0: 100.0%  MSE=4.01e-04
outlier, group-wise INT4 (g=128) Δ=0.0081  ordinary weights -> 0:  19.0%  MSE=1.57e-05

The setup is deliberately crude: take the matrix from cell 2 and multiply one input column (column 7) by 20 to stand in for an outlier channel. A report helper then looks only at the other, ordinary weights and prints the step size, the share rounded to exactly zero and the MSE for three setups: clean per-tensor INT4, per-tensor INT4 with the outlier, and group-wise INT4 (\(g = 128\)) with the outlier. Two bar charts put them side by side.

The first line says the outlier stretched the per-tensor step 15.0 times. Even the clean per-tensor case zeroes 27.9% of weights, higher than most people would guess. With the outlier, the step jumps from 0.0143 to 0.2148, 100.0% of ordinary weights become zero, and the MSE of 4.01e-04 equals the weights’ own variance (\(0.02^2\)). They’ve been wiped out. Group-wise INT4 keeps the damage to one group per row and lands at an MSE of 1.57e-05, slightly better than clean per-tensor. In both charts the red middle bar towers over the others, which is why 4-bit LLM weights are quantized group-wise.

Errors compound with depth

Each quantized layer adds its noise to an input that already carries the noise of every layer before it. Cell 4 measures how fast that builds up.

DEPTH, DIM = 24, 512
layers = [rng.normal(0.0, np.sqrt(2.0 / DIM), size=(DIM, DIM)) for _ in range(DEPTH)]  # He init keeps norms stable
x0 = rng.normal(size=(64, DIM))

def run_stack(ws: list[np.ndarray], x: np.ndarray) -> list[np.ndarray]:
    """Linear + ReLU blocks; returns the hidden state after every layer."""
    states = []
    for w in ws:
        x = np.maximum(x @ w, 0.0)
        states.append(x)
    return states

ref = run_stack(layers, x0)
curves = {}
for bits in (8, 4):
    q_states = run_stack([fake_quant(w, bits, 128) for w in layers], x0)
    curves[bits] = [np.linalg.norm(q - r) / np.linalg.norm(r) for q, r in zip(q_states, ref)]
    print(f"INT{bits} (g=128) relative error: layer 1 = {curves[bits][0]:.3f}, "
          f"layer 12 = {curves[bits][11]:.3f}, layer 24 = {curves[bits][-1]:.3f}")

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
for bits, c in zip((8, 4), ("steelblue", "crimson")):
    ax.plot(range(1, DEPTH + 1), curves[bits], marker="o", ms=3, color=c, label=f"INT{bits}")
ax.set(yscale="log", xlabel="layer", ylabel="relative error vs. full precision (log)",
       title="Rounding noise compounds with depth")
ax.legend(); plt.show()

INT8 (g=128) relative error: layer 1 = 0.006, layer 12 = 0.023, layer 24 = 0.032
INT4 (g=128) relative error: layer 1 = 0.115, layer 12 = 0.393, layer 24 = 0.477

Our stand-in for a model is a stack of 24 random 512 × 512 layers. They use He initialization (weights scaled by the square root of 2 over the layer width, which keeps activations a stable size). run_stack pushes 64 random inputs through them. Each layer is a matrix multiply followed by ReLU (rectified linear unit, which zeroes negative values). The cell runs the stack with full-precision, group-wise INT8 and group-wise INT4 weights, prints the relative error at layers 1, 12 and 24, and plots it for every layer.

INT8 barely moves: 0.006, 0.023, 0.032. INT4 goes 0.115, 0.393, 0.477, so by the last layer the hidden state is off by nearly half its own size, and its red line sits far above INT8’s. Residual connections and normalization damp this a lot in real transformers (it’s why 4-bit models work at all), but the direction is the same.

Reasoning compounds per-step errors

A chain of thought adds another kind of depth: steps. If a chain has \(n\) independent steps, each right with probability \(p\), the whole chain is right with probability

\[P(\text{chain correct}) = p^{\,n}\]

Cell 5 puts numbers on it.

steps = np.arange(1, 41)
for p in (0.99, 0.97, 0.95):
    print(f"per-step accuracy {p:.2f}: " + "  ".join(f"n={n:2d} -> {p ** n:5.1%}" for n in (5, 10, 20, 40)))

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
for p, c in zip((0.99, 0.97, 0.95), ("steelblue", "orange", "crimson")):
    ax.plot(steps, p ** steps, color=c, label=f"p = {p}")
ax.axvline(20, ls="--", color="grey", lw=1)
ax.set(xlabel="number of reasoning steps n", ylabel="P(whole chain correct) = pⁿ",
       title="Small per-step losses become large chain failures")
ax.legend(); plt.show()

per-step accuracy 0.99: n= 5 -> 95.1%  n=10 -> 90.4%  n=20 -> 81.8%  n=40 -> 66.9%
per-step accuracy 0.97: n= 5 -> 85.9%  n=10 -> 73.7%  n=20 -> 54.4%  n=40 -> 29.6%
per-step accuracy 0.95: n= 5 -> 77.4%  n=10 -> 59.9%  n=20 -> 35.8%  n=40 -> 12.9%

This one is pure arithmetic: the formula above for per-step accuracies of 99%, 97% and 95% at 5, 10, 20 and 40 steps, plus a plot of all three curves up to 40 steps.

At 99% per step, a 20-step chain is right 81.8% of the time. At 97%, only 54.4%. Two points lost per step become 27 points over 20 steps, and the curves keep pulling apart as chains get longer. Real steps aren’t independent, but this is how one quantized model can look fine on short benchmarks and worse at long maths and code.

What the evidence says

Liu et al. (2025) ran the first systematic study of quantized reasoning models, from 1.5B to 70B parameters, on AIME (the American Invitational Mathematics Examination), MATH-500 (500 competition maths problems), GPQA (Graduate-Level Google-Proof Q&A, a hard science benchmark) and LiveCodeBench (a coding benchmark). W8A8 and W4A16 came out close to lossless. Lower bit widths brought significant accuracy risks, with model size, origin and task difficulty deciding how much. And post-training quantization hurts more the more data a model was trained on (Kumar et al., 2024; Ouyang et al., 2024).

I call the result of naive post-hoc rounding “quantization shock” (my label, not a standard term): the network gets noisy weights after training ends and never gets a chance to adjust.

Why the industry takes the bet anyway

The bet on scale

So why does anyone quantize? Every new token means reading every weight from GPU memory once, with little arithmetic per weight, so at batch size 1 memory bandwidth is the speed limit:

\[\text{weight memory} = N_\text{params} \times \frac{b}{8}\ \text{bytes}, \qquad \text{tokens/s} \lesssim \frac{\text{memory bandwidth}}{\text{weight memory}}\]

Cell 6 runs those formulas for real hardware.

BANDWIDTH_TB_S, GPU_GB = 3.35, 80             # H100 SXM: HBM3 bandwidth and capacity
formats = {"FP16": 16, "FP8": 8, "INT4 (g=128)": 4 + 16 / 128}   # group-wise adds one FP16 scale per 128 weights

print(f"{'model':>5} {'format':>13} {'weights GB':>11} {'fits 80 GB?':>12} {'max tok/s @ batch 1':>20}")
for params_b in (7, 13, 70):
    for fmt, bits in formats.items():
        gb = params_b * 1e9 * bits / 8 / 1e9
        tok_s = BANDWIDTH_TB_S * 1e12 / (gb * 1e9)   # each new token reads every weight once
        print(f"{params_b:>4}B {fmt:>13} {gb:>11.1f} {'yes' if gb < GPU_GB else 'NO':>12} {tok_s:>20.0f}")
print("\n(weights only: the KV cache and activations need room on top of this)")

model        format  weights GB  fits 80 GB?  max tok/s @ batch 1
   7B          FP16        14.0          yes                  239
   7B           FP8         7.0          yes                  479
   7B  INT4 (g=128)         3.6          yes                  928
  13B          FP16        26.0          yes                  129
  13B           FP8        13.0          yes                  258
  13B  INT4 (g=128)         6.7          yes                  500
  70B          FP16       140.0           NO                   24
  70B           FP8        70.0          yes                   48
  70B  INT4 (g=128)        36.1          yes                   93

(weights only: the KV cache and activations need room on top of this)

No plot this time, just a table. The cell takes an NVIDIA H100 SXM (the server-module version of the card, with 80 GB of memory and 3.35 TB/s, terabytes per second, of bandwidth) and works out weight memory, whether it fits, and the speed ceiling in tokens per second for 7B, 13B and 70B models in FP16, FP8 and group-wise INT4. INT4 is counted as 4.125 bits per weight so the scales are included.

Look at the 70B rows. In FP16 the model needs 140.0 GB and doesn’t fit; in INT4 it needs 36.1 GB, leaves room for the KV cache, and its ceiling rises from 24 to 93 tokens/s. So on one card, your realistic options are a 13B model at full precision (26.0 GB) or a 70B model at 4 bits.

Which should you pick? Across more than 35,000 experiments on models from 19M to 176B parameters, holding total model bits fixed, Dettmers & Zettlemoyer found 4-bit precision “almost universally optimal” for zero-shot accuracy (accuracy on tasks the model wasn’t given examples for). The bigger, coarser model usually wins, because the rounding noise costs less than the extra parameters buy you.

Post-training quantization: the default

The cheapest way to make the bet is PTQ: quantize a finished 16-bit model, usually with a small calibration set and no retraining. It takes minutes to hours, which is why most quantized models you can download were made this way, and it’s much smarter than rounding to nearest:

  • GPTQ (Frantar et al., 2022), a PTQ method built for generative pre-trained transformers, quantizes one column at a time. It adjusts the remaining weights to cancel the error, using approximate second-order information.
  • AWQ (Activation-aware Weight Quantization, Lin et al., 2023) scales up the few weight channels that see large activations, so the weights that matter most lose the least.
  • SmoothQuant (Xiao et al., 2022) makes W8A8 practical by shifting the difficulty from activations into weights.
  • Rotation methods (QuaRot, Ashkboos et al., 2024; SpinQuant, Liu et al., 2024) spread outliers evenly across channels without changing the output.

SmoothQuant and the rotation methods are what handle activation outliers; QAT of the weights alone leaves them in place. PTQ’s real limitation is that the model never sees its own rounding error. At 8 bits or W4A16 that rarely matters. Below that, especially on long reasoning, it does.

Quantization-aware training: the frontier

QAT puts the rounding inside the training loop (Jacob et al., 2017). The model keeps full-precision master weights, and each step does three things:

  1. It runs the forward pass on fake-quantized weights (fake_quant from cell 2), so the loss sees what the deployed model will see.
  2. It passes the gradient straight through the rounding. round() has zero gradient almost everywhere, so the straight-through estimator, or STE (Bengio et al., 2013), treats it as the identity, \(\partial \hat w / \partial w \approx 1\), and applies the gradient for \(\hat w\) to \(w\).
  3. It updates the master weights, which drift in full precision until they cross a rounding boundary and, over training, settle into values that survive the grid.

Cell 7 compares PTQ and QAT head to head.

data_rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
X = data_rng.normal(size=(2048, 8))                  # toy regression task from a random "teacher" network
teacher = [data_rng.normal(0, 1.2 / np.sqrt(m), (m, n)) for m, n in ((8, 32), (32, 1))]
y = np.tanh(X @ teacher[0]) @ teacher[1] + 0.01 * data_rng.normal(size=(2048, 1))
X_tr, y_tr, X_te, y_te = X[:1536], y[:1536], X[1536:], y[1536:]
QAT_BITS = 4

def forward(ws: list[np.ndarray], bs: list[np.ndarray], x: np.ndarray) -> list[np.ndarray]:
    acts = [x]
    for i, (w, b) in enumerate(zip(ws, bs)):
        z = acts[-1] @ w + b
        acts.append(np.tanh(z) if i < len(ws) - 1 else z)
    return acts

def train(bits: int | None, steps: int = 800, lr: float = 3e-3) -> tuple[list, list]:
    init = np.random.default_rng(2)
    sizes = [8, 64, 64, 1]
    ws = [init.normal(0, 1 / np.sqrt(m), (m, n)) for m, n in zip(sizes, sizes[1:])]   # FP32 master weights
    bs = [np.zeros(n) for n in sizes[1:]]
    params = ws + bs
    m1, m2 = [np.zeros_like(p) for p in params], [np.zeros_like(p) for p in params]
    for t in range(1, steps + 1):
        wq = [fake_quant(w, bits) if bits else w for w in ws]     # forward pass sees the INT grid
        acts = forward(wq, bs, X_tr)
        g = 2 * (acts[-1] - y_tr) / len(X_tr)
        grads_w, grads_b = [], []
        for i in reversed(range(len(wq))):
            if i < len(wq) - 1:
                g = g * (1 - acts[i + 1] ** 2)
            grads_w.insert(0, acts[i].T @ g); grads_b.insert(0, g.sum(0))
            g = g @ wq[i].T
        # STE: treat round() as identity, so dL/dW_quant is applied straight to the master weights
        for p, gr, a, b_ in zip(params, grads_w + grads_b, m1, m2):
            a[:] = 0.9 * a + 0.1 * gr; b_[:] = 0.999 * b_ + 0.001 * gr ** 2
            p -= lr * (a / (1 - 0.9 ** t)) / (np.sqrt(b_ / (1 - 0.999 ** t)) + 1e-8)
    return ws, bs

def test_mse(ws: list, bs: list, bits: int | None) -> float:
    wq = [fake_quant(w, bits) if bits else w for w in ws]
    return float(np.mean((forward(wq, bs, X_te)[-1] - y_te) ** 2))

fp_ws, fp_bs = train(bits=None)
qat_ws, qat_bs = train(bits=QAT_BITS)
scores = {"FP32 baseline": test_mse(fp_ws, fp_bs, None),
          f"PTQ INT{QAT_BITS} (round after training)": test_mse(fp_ws, fp_bs, QAT_BITS),
          f"QAT INT{QAT_BITS} (STE, fake-quant in loop)": test_mse(qat_ws, qat_bs, QAT_BITS)}
for k, v in scores.items():
    print(f"{k:<38} test MSE = {v:.4f}   ({v / scores['FP32 baseline']:.1f}x baseline)")

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.bar(["FP32\nbaseline", f"PTQ\nINT{QAT_BITS}", f"QAT\nINT{QAT_BITS}"], list(scores.values()),
       color=["grey", "crimson", "seagreen"])
ax.set(ylabel="test MSE", title="Training with the grid in the loop recovers most of the loss")
plt.show()

PTQ INT4 (round after training)        test MSE = 0.0294   (9.5x baseline)

This snippet builds a toy regression task (targets from a small random “teacher” network, with 1,536 training and 512 test examples) and a student MLP (multi-layer perceptron) with layers of 8, 64, 64 and 1 units and tanh (hyperbolic tangent) activations. The student is trained twice from the same starting weights, for 800 steps of the Adam optimizer: once in full precision, and once with QAT, using fake-quantized INT4 weights and the STE. Then the cell tests the float model, that model rounded to INT4 (PTQ), and the QAT model.

Three numbers come out. The FP32 (32-bit floating point) baseline scores a test MSE of 0.0031, PTQ at INT4 rises to 0.0294 (9.5 times the baseline), and QAT at INT4 reaches 0.0052, just 1.7 times. In the chart, the red PTQ bar towers over the other two. Same bits, same architecture: the only difference is that one model saw the grid while it learned.

Real releases follow suit. Google’s Gemma 3 QAT checkpoints shrink the 27B model from 54 GB in BF16 to 14.1 GB in int4. Meta’s quantized Llama 3.2 shipped QAT with LoRA (low-rank adaptation) adaptors as its high-accuracy option. Moonshot’s Kimi K2 Thinking applied INT4 weight-only QAT during post-training because long reasoning traces made ordinary quantization lose too much. My rule of thumb: PTQ when the model is finished, QAT when the low-bit model is the product.

Mixed-precision QAT: spending bits where they matter

Not every layer is equally sensitive. The token embedding and the LM head (the language-model head, which turns the final hidden state into word probabilities) sit right on the path from input tokens to output, so their errors reach everything downstream. The middle blocks hold most of the parameters but only add updates to the residual stream, and much of their capacity is redundant. So mixed-precision schemes keep the embeddings and head at BF16, FP8 or INT8 and push the middle blocks to INT4, sometimes INT3 (3-bit integers). Below that, the training changes character: ParetoQ (Liu et al., 2025) found that at 3 bits and above, quantized models stay close to their pre-trained distributions, while at 2 bits and below the representations change drastically.

The recipe has three steps. Measure each layer’s sensitivity by quantizing it alone, hand out bits under a fixed average budget, then run QAT with that bit map. Cell 8 does the first two.

N_LAYERS, D, ALPHA = 12, 512, 0.2
stack = [rng.normal(0.0, np.sqrt(2.0 / D), size=(D, D)) for _ in range(N_LAYERS)]
x_in = rng.normal(size=(64, D))

def run_residual(ws: list[np.ndarray], x: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
    """Transformer-shaped toy: input projection -> residual blocks -> output head."""
    h = x @ ws[0]                                   # "embedding": on the direct path
    for w in ws[1:-1]:
        h = h + ALPHA * np.maximum(h @ w, 0.0)      # middle blocks write small updates to a residual stream
    return h @ ws[-1]                               # "LM head": on the direct path

ref_out = run_residual(stack, x_in)

def stack_error(bits_per_layer: list[int | None]) -> float:
    ws = [w if b is None else fake_quant(w, b, 128) for w, b in zip(stack, bits_per_layer)]
    out = run_residual(ws, x_in)
    return float(np.linalg.norm(out - ref_out) / np.linalg.norm(ref_out))

# 1) sensitivity: push ONE layer to INT3, keep the rest in full precision
sens = [stack_error([3 if j == i else None for j in range(N_LAYERS)]) for i in range(N_LAYERS)]
# 2) same 4.0-bit average budget: 2 layers @ 8, 2 @ 4, 8 @ 3 = 48 bits = 12 x 4
order = np.argsort(sens)[::-1]
alloc = [3] * N_LAYERS
for rank, i in enumerate(order[:4]):
    alloc[i] = 8 if rank < 2 else 4
print("sensitivity (INT3, one layer):", " ".join(f"{s:.3f}" for s in sens))
print("mixed bits per layer:         ", alloc, f"avg = {np.mean(alloc):.2f}")
print(f"uniform INT4 output error = {stack_error([4] * N_LAYERS):.3f}")
print(f"mixed    (avg 4 bits)     = {stack_error(alloc):.3f}")

bar_colors = {8: "seagreen", 4: "orange", 3: "crimson"}

for b, c in bar_colors.items():

       title="Sensitivity scan decides where the bits go")

The toy here is shaped like a transformer: an input projection (“emb”), ten middle blocks that each add a 0.2-scaled ReLU update to a running hidden state, and an output projection (“head”). stack_error quantizes chosen layers group-wise and returns the final output’s relative error. The cell pushes one layer at a time to INT3 to measure sensitivity, then gives INT8 to the two most sensitive layers, INT4 to the next two and INT3 to the rest, an average of exactly 4 bits (\(2 \times 8 + 2 \times 4 + 8 \times 3 = 12 \times 4\)). It prints the results and plots each layer’s sensitivity, coloured by its bits.

The sensitivities tell the story. “emb” scores 0.183 and “head” 0.287, against 0.035 to 0.050 for the middle blocks, so the scan finds the input and output projections without being told. The allocation comes out as [8, 3, 3, 3, 3, 3, 3, 3, 3, 4, 4, 8], averaging 4.00. Uniform INT4 gives an output error of 0.157; the mixed allocation gives 0.116, about 26% less for the same memory. In this toy the sensitivity comes purely from where a layer sits; real models have to be measured one by one, but the method is the same.

Other methods in brief

High-precision cloud serving

In datacenters, FP8 (Micikevicius et al., 2022) is a common alternative to integer weights. It keeps an exponent, so it follows the dynamic range of weights and activations better than INT8. It also runs natively on NVIDIA’s Hopper generation (the H100’s) and typically serves close to BF16 quality. Blackwell, the next generation, adds 4-bit floating-point formats with a shared scale per small block: MXFP4 (microscaling 4-bit floating point, Rouhani et al., 2023) and NVFP4, NVIDIA’s own 4-bit floating-point format. OpenAI’s gpt-oss-120b ships its MoE (mixture-of-experts) weights in MXFP4, which is how it runs on one 80 GB GPU, and NVFP4 now works even for pretraining (NVIDIA, 2025).

KV-cache quantization

The model stores the attention keys and values for every token it has seen. On long contexts, that cache can outgrow the weights. Quantizing it to FP8 or lower frees memory for longer contexts and more users without touching the weights, and KIVI (Liu et al., 2024) gets all the way down to 2 bits by quantizing keys per channel and values per token, with 2.6× less peak memory and up to 4× larger batches.

Edge and on-device models

On laptops and phones memory is the hard limit, so 4-bit is the default. GGUF, the model file format used by llama.cpp, holds formats like the q4_K_M from the top of this post, mostly made with PTQ. QAT checkpoints are arriving too: Gemma 3’s QAT models ship as Q4_0 GGUFs (llama.cpp’s basic 4-bit format), and Meta’s quantized Llama 3.2 targets phones with a reported 56% smaller model and 2 to 4× faster inference.

Try it yourself, and what to take away

This last experiment runs on your own computer rather than in Colab. With Ollama installed and around 16 GB of RAM (random-access memory), give one multi-step maths problem to the same model in three forms:

ollama run gemma3:4b-it-fp16     # 16-bit reference (8.6 GB)
ollama run gemma3:4b-it-q4_K_M   # 4-bit, post-training quantized (3.4 GB)
ollama run gemma3:4b-it-qat      # 4-bit, quantization-aware trained (4.0 GB)

If you keep four things from this post, make it these:

  • Each weight moves by at most \(\Delta/2\), and \(\Delta\) is set by the largest value on the grid, so one outlier can erase a per-tensor INT4 matrix. Group-wise scales contain it.
  • Per-step losses compound (\(0.99^{20} \approx 82\%\), \(0.97^{20} \approx 54\%\)), so reasoning shows the damage first.
  • Generation is bandwidth-bound, so at fixed memory a bigger 4-bit model usually beats a smaller 16-bit one.
  • Most models ship with PTQ. Labs that need 4-bit models to keep reasoning use QAT, increasingly in mixed precision.

So yes, quantization degrades reasoning. It’s still the standard because, done well, the parameters it buys are worth more than the precision it costs.
